blocks.text: Propositional logic is a basic form of logic used in computer science. It deals with statements that can be true or false. These statements are called propositions (as shown in Figure 2.3)

blocks.alt: Four statements, each with an arrow to its truth value: 2 + 3 = 5 is True, The sky is blue is True, 1 > 3 is False, Today is Sunday is False.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.3: Propositional Logic Statements (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.3).

blocks.title: Do You Know?
blocks.text: Propositional logic is the simplest type of logic, but it forms the base of all computer reasoning!

A proposition is a statement that is either true or false. It cannot be both true and false at the same time. Questions and commands are not propositions. For example, “The sun rises in the east” is a proposition. A proposition must have a clear meaning. It should not be confusing. Propositions are the basic units of logic. They are used to form logical expressions. Understanding propositions is important in logic. A proposition is usually represented by a capital letter, such as P, Q, or R. For example, if p represents the statement “The sky is blue”, then we write:

A simple proposition contains only one statement. It cannot be broken into smaller parts. For example, “It is raining” is a simple proposition. A compound proposition is formed by combining two or more simple propositions. Logical connectives are used to join them. For example, “It is raining and it is cold” is a compound proposition. Compound propositions can express complex ideas. They are common in logical reasoning. Both types are important in propositional logic.

Logical connectives are words used to connect propositions. AND is used when both statements must be true. OR is used when at least one statement is true. NOT is used to reverse the truth of a statement. These connectives help form compound propositions. They are commonly used in computer programs. Logical connectives help in decision-making (as shown in Figure 2.4). They make logical expressions clear. Understanding them is essential in logic.

blocks.alt: Three rows. AND: circles A and B, an arrow headed A and B, True if both A and B are true, and a Venn diagram with only the overlap shaded. OR: circles A and B, an arrow headed A or B, True if A or B is true (or both), and a Venn diagram with both circles shaded. NOT: circle A, an arrow headed Not A, True if A is false, and circle A struck through.
